food.text: In 2010, UNESCO recognized Mexico's cuisine as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity. The tradition it honors reaches back to the Olmec and Maya, who domesticated maize and created the standard process of nixtamalization.

The number of tortilla factories in Mexico grew from 2,214 in 1945 to 23,216 in 1980. Tortilla purchases shifted from small tortillerias to mass producers, helping companies such as Gruma and its American subsidiary Mission Foods to grow.

A drop in global corn production in 2006 to 2007 sharply raised tortilla prices in Mexico and set off protests known as the Tortilla Crisis. In response, President Felipe Calderón introduced the Tortilla Price Stabilization Pact, in which several producers agreed to a price ceiling.

Tortilla sales boomed in the United States in the early 21st century. They reached $6 billion in 2006, with an annual growth rate of 9%, and $9 billion in 2009. In the United Kingdom, wheat tortilla sales rose 17% in 2010.

In 1982 a group of women chefs and other culinary experts created the Mexican Culinary Circle of Mexico City. They acted from fear that traditions would be lost as foreign techniques and foods increasingly arrived, and the group is seen as the start of a movement to preserve authentic Mexican food.

In her 1972 book The Cuisines of Mexico, Diana Kennedy drew a sharp distinction between Mexican food and Tex-Mex. Robb Walsh of the Houston Press called it a breakthrough cookbook that treated the food of the poor with the same respect as the food of the upper classes.

The Bracero Program (1942 to 1964) brought temporary employment to millions of Mexican migrant workers, particularly in labor-intensive industries in Southwestern states. With them came an increase in Mexican food in regions that had previously seen little ethnic influence from Mexico.

Even as tortillas won new markets abroad, Mexicans ate fewer corn tortillas at home. The source reports daily average consumption falling from 249 kilograms in 2002 to 157 kilograms in 2010 as consumers shifted to other foods.

Felix Tijerina was born in 1905 and moved to Houston in 1922, where he began as a busboy at the Original Mexican Restaurant. He opened the Mexican Inn in 1929 and later became national president of LULAC from 1956 to 1960. His chain of Felix Mexican Restaurants promoted Tex-Mex until 2008.

In 2013, Carlos Gaytán became the first Mexican to obtain a Michelin star, for his work at the Mexique restaurant in Chicago. A year later, Daniela Soto-Innes helped open Cosme in New York City, serving as its chef de cuisine.

Jamaican cuisine spread with migration as Jamaican merchants and labourers settled in coastal Latin America. They worked in agriculture and in building railroads, ports and the Panama Canal, and contributed Jamaican dishes to the region.

art.text: After the Mexican Revolution, the government funded a huge art project that turned the walls of public buildings into scenes of Mexico's past, present, and future. The murals carried social, political, and historical messages meant to reshape how Mexicans understood their nation's history. Orozco, who had fought in the war, painted its horrors rather than glorifying it, and his murals were heavily criticized and even defaced.

From the 1920s, the muralist project was headed by three artists known as "The Big Three": Diego Rivera, José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros. Their tradition continues in Mexico today and inspired the Chicano art movement in the United States.

Luis Barragán is named as the most notable architect of the mid-20th century in Mexico. Architects of this era combined functionalism, regionalism, and modernism to create a distinctive Mexican style.

Siqueiros was exiled from Mexico to the US in 1932 and moved to Los Angeles, where he painted three murals. Two were painted over, but América Tropical survived. The Getty Conservation Institute restored it, and the América Tropical Interpretive Center opened to give the public access.

Orozco was the first of the Big Three to paint in the US, creating murals at Pomona College in the late 1920s. Rivera lived in the United States from 1930 to 1934 and staged an influential show of his easel work at the Museum of Modern Art.

At Ciudad Universitaria, the Rectory of 1952 includes murals by David Alfaro Siqueiros. The Science Building features José Chávez Morado's mural The Conquest of Energy, and Rivera made a relief for the new Estadio Olímpico Universitario in 1952.

Mexico's first project of high-density, low-cost housing was the Centro Urbano Alemán, built in Mexico City between 1947 and 1949. It was designed by Mario Pani, who later helped direct the Ciudad Universitaria project.

Director Paul Leduc specialized in films without dialogue and became known in the 1970s. His first major success was Reed: Insurgent Mexico in 1971, followed by Frida in 1984, a biography of Frida Kahlo.

war.text: The Caste War of Yucatán began in 1847 with a revolt of Indigenous Maya against Hispanic Yucatecos, and it is described as one of the most successful modern Native American revolts. War and armed struggle continued for more than 50 years, and an estimated 40,000 to 50,000 people died in the hostilities. Its formal end came only in 1915, and skirmishes with settlements that rejected Mexican control continued until 1933.

On January 1, 1994, the day the North American Free Trade Agreement came into effect, the Maya Zapatista Army (EZLN) issued its First Declaration from the Lacandon Jungle. It effectively declared war on the Mexican government, which it considered illegitimate because it was out of touch with the will of the people.

The formal end of the Caste War came in 1915, when Mexican forces led by Yucatán Governor Salvador Alvarado subdued the territory. Alvarado introduced reforms from the Mexican Revolution that ended some Maya grievances. By then war and armed struggle had gone on in one form or another for more than 50 years, and an estimated 40,000 to 50,000 people had died in the hostilities.

The Mexican Revolution of 1910 to 1920 was a ten-year civil war. Pressures on Indigenous communities and their lands, which had grown under Porfirio Díaz, exploded in certain areas of Mexico during that war.

The last time the Mexican army felt it had to take a village by force that had never recognized Mexican law was in April 1933. Five Maya and two Mexican soldiers died in the battle for the village of Dzula, the last skirmish of a conflict lasting more than 85 years.
The EZLN said it chose armed struggle because peaceful protest had achieved too little. It named sit-ins and marches as the peaceful means that had failed to produce results.

In 2021, the governments of Mexico and Guatemala apologized to the Maya people for the repression and war of extermination carried out by both states. The source describes that war as having lasted almost 50 years.

literature.text: Cuban literature is written in Spanish, on the island or abroad by Cubans. Nicolás Guillén focused on literature as social protest. Dulce María Loynaz, José Lezama Lima and Alejo Carpentier instead dealt with more personal or universal issues.

Cuban literature has recently seen a so-called "boom" among authors born in the 1950s and '60s. Many of these writers felt compelled to continue their work in exile because of perceived censorship by the Cuban authorities. Many of them fled abroad during the 1990s.

Oral literature in many Indigenous Mesoamerican languages kept being transmitted to this day. Ethnologists began collecting it at the beginning of the 20th century. However, their work did not promote native language literacy in the communities where they worked.

Cuba's years from 1971 to 1975 are known as the "Quinquenio Gris", roughly the "Five-year Grey Period". The National Congress of Education and Culture, held from April 23 to April 30, 1971, set out to abolish the inquisitive and questioning role of literature. This had negative consequences for short story writing.
tags: National Congress of Education and Culture

literature.text: Reinaldo Arenas and Guillermo Cabrera Infante earned international recognition in the postrevolutionary era of Cuban literature. They are named alongside other writers who dealt with personal or universal issues rather than social protest.

Cuban authors of the exile generation scattered across the world. Daína Chaviano went to the USA, Zoé Valdés to France, Eliseo Alberto to Mexico and Abilio Estévez to Spain. Pedro Juan Gutiérrez and Antonio Orlando Rodríguez are listed as still in Cuba.

For most of the 20th century, Mexican educational policy focused on Hispanicization, teaching only Spanish and discouraging Indigenous languages. As a result, one scholar estimated in 1983 that no group of Nahuatl speakers had attained general literacy in Nahuatl.

Despite the Quinquenio Gris, books still appeared in Cuba. They included El fin del caos llega quietamente (1971) by Ángel Arango, Onoloria (1973) by Miguel Collazo, Los testigos (1973) by Joel James and Caballito blanco (1974) by Onelio Jorge Cardoso.

From 1966 to 1970, many Cuban short story collections were written. They included Condenados de Condado (1968) by Norberto Fuentes, Tiempo de cambio (1969) by Manuel Cofiño and Los pasos en la hierba (1970) by Eduardo Heras León.

Returning native language literacy to Indigenous peoples is described as an important and extremely difficult job in Mesoamerica today. According to the article, it is only beginning to be undertaken.

Nahuatl is spoken by over 1 million people, with approximately 10% of speakers monolingual. It is not considered endangered as a whole. Even so, during the late 20th century several Nahuatl dialects became extinct.

Cuban short story writing kept growing in the 1980s. Senel Paz published El niño aquel in 1980, and Abel Prieto Jiménez published Noche de sábado in 1989. Aida Bahr's Ofelias appears among the relevant books of the decade.

science.text: After the Mexican Revolution, a ten-year civil war, Mexico made significant progress in science and technology. During the 20th century, new universities such as the National Polytechnic Institute and the Monterrey Institute of Technology were founded. Research institutes, such as those at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, were founded as well.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico

science.text: According to the World Bank, Mexico is Latin America's largest exporter of high-technology goods. This puts the country at the top of the region for manufactured goods that involve high levels of research and development.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico

science.text: Ricardo Miledi, one of the ten most quoted neuro-biologists of all time, was born in Mexico City in 1927. His science career began in 1955, just before he graduated in medicine at UNAM, when he joined one of the most active research groups in Mexico. It was part of the National Institute of Cardiology.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico

science.text: UNAM provides education in science, medicine, and engineering, and most of Mexico's new research institutes were created within it. Twelve institutes were integrated into UNAM from 1929 to 1973. This made it one of the most important centers of higher learning in the country.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico

science.text: American anthropologist William T. Sanders surveyed Teotihuacan from 1960 to 1964. The results were published in 1965 as The Cultural Ecology of the Teotihuacan Valley. He later turned his attention south to Kaminaljuyu in Guatemala, partly because of evidence of links between that Mayan site and Teotihuacan.
tags: The Cultural Ecology of the Teotihuacan Valley

science.text: In 1961, the Center for Research and Advanced Studies of the National Polytechnic Institute was established for graduate studies in subjects such as biology, mathematics, and physics. That year its graduate programs in physics and mathematics began. Schools of science were also established in Puebla, San Luis Potosí, Monterrey, Veracruz, and Michoacán.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico
tags: Center for Research and Advanced Studies

science.text: Mexico's national science bodies took shape in the late 1960s and early 1970s. The Academy for Scientific Research was established in 1968. The National Council of Science and Technology (CONAHCYT) followed in 1971.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico
tags: National Council of Science and Technology

science.text: In 1979, The Basin of Mexico: Ecological Processes in the Evolution of a Civilization was published, co-authored by Sanders. It was a regional analysis that synthesised multiple survey results spanning 3000 years. Because of its bright green cover and influence, it has been nicknamed "The Green Bible".
In 2019, CONACYT's new PRONACES initiative, aimed at funding research on local societal issues, accounted for just 1.1% of the council's budget, though resources may be reassigned to it in future.
science.source_title: History of science and technology in Mexico

science.text: During the 1980s and 1990s, William T. Sanders co-directed survey work at the Classic Maya site of Copán in Honduras. In 1985, he was elected to the National Academy of Sciences. He also served as a visiting professor at institutions in Mexico, including UNAM.

politics.text: From 1920 to 1946, Mexico was led by revolutionary generals serving as presidents, including Álvaro Obregón, Plutarco Elías Calles, Lázaro Cárdenas and Manuel Avila Camacho. The government of this post-revolutionary period sought to bring order and end military intervention in politics.

Mexico entered World War II in response to German attacks on Mexican ships. On May 13, 1942, German submarine U-564 attacked and crippled the tanker Potrero del Llano, killing 13 of its 35 crewmen. On May 21, U-160 attacked and sunk the tanker Faja de Oro, killing 10 of its 37 crewmen. After the torpedoing of the two ships, Mexico declared war on Germany, Italy and Japan on May 30, 1942.
politics.source_title: Latin America during World War II

politics.text: Denmark responded to doubts about its Greenland claim by seeking diplomatic agreements recognizing its sovereignty. The first was the 1917 treaty selling the Danish Virgin Islands to the United States.

After a period of violent open conflict over religious matters, Mexico's Church-state relations returned to a modus vivendi, while the anticlerical constitutional framework remained in place. A new constitutional framework was created in 1992, which reiterated the separation between the Catholic Church and the state. It lifted most but not all restrictions on religious freedom and on the activities of the Catholic Church in Mexico.

The Institutional Revolutionary Party built its power by bringing organized groups inside it. Workers, peasants and office workers were incorporated as sectors of the single party, and for a short period so was the army.

As president from 1920 to 1924, Álvaro Obregón instigated land reform and strengthened organized labor. He also won recognition from the United States and settled claims with companies and individuals that had lost property during the Revolution.

During World War II, Panama was the most important Latin American nation for the Allies because of the Panama Canal, which linked the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans. To protect the canal and combat Axis influence, the United States expanded its interests in the region through Lend-Lease and similar programs.
politics.source_title: Latin America during World War II

politics.text: Plutarco Elías Calles provoked a major conflict with the Catholic Church and Catholic guerrilla armies when he enforced the anticlerical articles of the constitution. The article does not give casualty figures for this fighting. The conflict ended with an agreement.

The constitution prohibited presidential reelection, but Álvaro Obregón wished to run again, so it was amended to allow non-consecutive re-election. He won the 1928 elections but was assassinated by a Catholic activist, which caused a succession crisis.

Álvaro Obregón won the 1928 elections after the constitution was amended to allow non-consecutive re-election, but a Catholic activist assassinated him. The killing caused a succession crisis, and Calles responded by founding the Institutional Revolutionary Party, which dominated Mexico for the rest of the 20th century.

The Potrero del Llano was an Italian tanker that the Mexican government seized in port in April 1941. German submarine U-564 attacked and crippled it on May 13, 1942, killing 13 of its 35 crewmen. On May 21, 1942, a second seized Italian tanker, the Faja de Oro, was attacked and sunk by U-160, killing 10 of its 37 crewmen.
politics.source_title: Latin America during World War II

politics.text: The Mexican Revolution, lasting roughly from 1910 to 1920, was a decade-long conflict that killed about 900,000 of Mexico's 15 million people. The 1921 census reported a loss of about 1 million inhabitants, in a country that had held a little more than 13 million people in 1900.

philosophy.text: Palo, also called Las Reglas de Congo, developed in Cuba in the late 19th or early 20th century. It draws heavily on the traditional Kongo religion of Central Africa, with added influences from Catholicism and Spiritism.

Enrique Dussel was an Argentine-Mexican philosopher, historian and theologian. In the events leading up to Argentina's military dictatorship of 1976–1983, he was increasingly the target of violence, including death threats, the bombing of his house and sacking from the university. He escaped to Mexico in 1975 as a political exile, where he continued working as a professor of philosophy.

Alfredo López Austin was a Mexican historian who wrote extensively on the Aztec worldview and on Mesoamerican religion. He studied law and worked as a lawyer in Ciudad Juárez before an academic career at UNAM that lasted some fifty years. In 2020 he won the National Prize for Arts and Sciences in Fine Arts.

Dussel produced some forty books on subjects including the philosophy of liberation, ethics, political economy, theology and modernity/postmodernity. Much of his work is only limitedly available in English, and some contend it has not received the broader attention it warrants.

In Palo, the central object is the nganga, usually an iron cauldron. It contains sticks and human remains called nfumbe, meaning the spirit of that dead person inhabits it and serves its owner. The bones are traditionally dug up from a graveyard at night, and the most important is the skull, called the kiyumba. The palero commands the nganga to heal, but also to cause harm, including misfortune, illness and death. Ngangas judías are capable of murder, and are fed the keeper's own blood and animal blood.

Dussel returned to Argentina in 1969 and was influenced by dependency theory and the writings of Emmanuel Levinas, both of which became major influences on his thinking. Earlier, in Israel between 1959 and 1961, he had worked at a cooperative led by the French Jesuit Paul Gauthier, who shaped his view of liberation theology.

Alfredo López Austin co-wrote Monte sagrado – Templo Mayor with his son, the archaeologist Leonardo López Luján, in 2009. The book examines the hill and the pyramid in Mesoamerican religious tradition. His earlier work with López Luján, from 1999, explored the Feathered Serpent and Mesoamerican transformations.

Trinidadian Marxist C. L. R. James wrote The Black Jacobins (1938) about the Haitian Revolution. Together with Sartre and Aimé Cesaire, he influenced Frantz Fanon, author of Black Skin, White Masks (1952). The Caribbean Philosophical Association awards the Frantz Fanon prize.

Palo practitioners often call their religious homeland Ngola. This reflects a belief in the historical Kingdom of Kongo as Palo's place of origin, a place where the spirits are more powerful. Palo also draws on other African traditions in Cuba, such as the West African Yoruba.

Dussel's 1990 book El último Marx (1863–1882) y la liberación latinoamericana offered a commentary on the third and fourth drafts of Marx's Capital. It links Marx's late writing to Latin American liberation, a theme central to Dussel's philosophy.

culture.text: The Golden Age of Mexican cinema, between 1935 and 1959, was the period when the quality and economic success of the country's films reached their peak. Actors such as Cantinflas and Pedro Infante appeared on the silver screen, and actresses Dolores del Río and María Félix became icons.
Mexico hosted the Summer Olympic Games in 1968 and the FIFA World Cup in 1970 and 1986. With the 2026 World Cup, it is set to become the first country to host the FIFA World Cup three times.

Festivals like Día de Muertos celebrate indigenous traditions alongside Catholic rituals. Mexican cuisine likewise builds on indigenous ingredients like maize and chili peppers in beloved dishes such as tacos and mole.

According to the Mexican census, Roman Catholicism was practiced by 77.7 percent of Mexicans in 2020. In many parts of the country, Catholic Christianity is heavily syncretized with folk customs, as well as Aztec, Mayan, and other Mesoamerican religions.

Roman Catholicism is the dominant religion in Mexico, practiced by 77.7 percent of the population in 2020. In many parts of the country it is heavily syncretized with folk customs and with Aztec, Mayan and other Mesoamerican religions, so old and new beliefs blend together.

Palo is a religion that developed in Cuba in the late 19th or early 20th century, drawing heavily on traditional Kongo religion. Its central object is the nganga, a vessel usually made from an iron cauldron, which is regarded as inhabited by the spirit of a dead person whose bones are placed inside it. The nganga is fed with the blood of sacrificed animals such as dogs, pigs, goats and cockerels. Palo practitioners have faced problems with law enforcement for robbing graves to obtain human bones for their nganga.

The traditional national sport of Mexico is Charrería, a series of equestrian events, and its national horse is the Azteca. Bullfighting, a tradition brought from Spain, is also popular, and Mexico City's Plaza México, the world's largest bullfighting venue, seats 48,000 people.

Mexico's Jewish community founded most of its social and religious organizations in the first half of the 20th century. In 1918 it opened the first federally recognized synagogue under the terms of the Constitution of 1917, and the Colegio Israelita de México followed in 1924.
culture.source_title: History of the Jews in Mexico

culture.text: Cuban artists were incorporating Palo imagery into their work by the start of the 21st century. José Bedia Valdés received the mpungu Sarabanda at his initiation into Palo, and Leonardo Padura Fuentes' 2001 novel Adiós Hemingway also includes Palo. Initiation into Palo is done by rayamiento, or "cutting": the initiate is cut with a razor blade, rooster's spur or thorn on the chest, back, hands, legs or tongue. Their blood is given to the nganga, and the cuts sometimes leave scars.
The date 13 March 1325 was chosen in 1925 to celebrate the 600th anniversary of Tenochtitlan. The exact date of the city's founding is actually unclear.

The location of the Templo Mayor was rediscovered in the early 20th century, but major excavations did not take place until 1978–1982, after utility workers came across a massive stone disc depicting the nude dismembered body of the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui. The disc is 3.25 meters in diameter and is held at the Templo Mayor Museum. The Spanish had dismantled the temple complex and built the central district of their colonial city on top of it, destroying the great temple during construction of a cathedral.

The first printing press for the Hebrew alphabet was brought to Mexico in 1930. Jewish newspapers appeared in several languages, including the Yiddish Mexicanisher Idish Leben in 1927 and Di shtime in 1935.
culture.source_title: History of the Jews in Mexico

culture.text: The archaeological evidence indicates that the Maya never formed a united empire. They were organized into small chiefdoms that were constantly at war, and López Austin and López Luján said the Preclassic Maya were bellicose and probably had a greater mastery of the art of war than Teotihuacan. Even so, the idea that the Maya were a peaceful society given to religious contemplation was particularly promoted by early and mid-20th century Mayanists such as Sylvanus G. Morley and J. Eric S. Thompson. Confirmation that the Maya practiced human sacrifice and ritual cannibalism came much later, for example from the murals of Bonampak.

In 1918, the first federally recognized synagogue was established under the terms of Mexico's Constitution of 1917. In the same period Jewish communities founded religious schools, including the first K'tav in 1917 and the first Ashkenazi religious school in 1922.
culture.source_title: History of the Jews in Mexico

culture.text: Jewish religious and cultural life in Mexico grew with its own press. The Yiddish newspaper Mexicanisher Idish Leben appeared in 1927 and Der Veg in 1929. In 1930 the first printing press for the Hebrew alphabet was brought to Mexico.
culture.source_title: History of the Jews in Mexico
